## The CIRCT tool tour {#tools-route}

This section follows the [ARITH 2026 CIRCT Tutorial](https://github.com/cowardsa/CIRCT_TUTORIAL_2026) by Samuel Coward and myself.

::: {.incremental}
1. **Basics:** `circt-verilog`, `circt-opt`, `circt-lec`, and `firtool`.

2. **Synthesis & Reports:** `circt-synth`, AIGER export, and area estimation.
:::

## Start the environment {#tools-setup}

Pull and enter the pre-built course image:

```bash
docker run -it ghcr.io/bynaryman/mlir-summer-school-2026-circt:latest
```
\

The same image can be built locally:
```bash
git clone https://github.com/Bynaryman/MLIR_ACM_Summer_School_2026_CIRCT
cd tutorial
docker build -t mlir-summer-school-2026-circt .
docker run -it mlir-summer-school-2026-circt
```
\


::: {.fragment}
Quick check:
```bash
circt-opt --version
LLVM version 23.0.0git
CIRCT firtool-1.147.0
```
:::

## Tutorial Part 1: CIRCT basics {#tools-basics}

::: {.incremental}
1. Compile a SystemVerilog design to CIRCT IR.

2. Apply CIRCT optimization passes.

3. Verify that a transformation preserved the circuit.

4. Generate SystemVerilog for downstream EDA tools.
:::

## Compile the FMA example {#tools-compile}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
```systemverilog
// rtl/fma.sv
module fma (
  input  wire [3:0] a,
  input  wire [3:0] b,
  input  wire [3:0] c,
  output wire [8:0] d
);
  assign d = (a * b) + (c * 1'd1);
endmodule
```
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
```bash
circt-verilog rtl/fma.sv
```

`circt-verilog` parses SystemVerilog and prints CIRCT IR.

SystemVerilog support remains an ongoing effort documented by
[`sv-tests`](https://chipsalliance.github.io/sv-tests-results/).
:::
::::

## The imported CIRCT IR {#tools-compiled-ir}

```mlir
module {
  hw.module @fma(
      in %a : i4, in %b : i4, in %c : i4,
      out d : i9) {
    %c0_i5 = hw.constant 0 : i5
    %0 = comb.concat %c0_i5, %a : i5, i4
    %1 = comb.concat %c0_i5, %b : i5, i4
    %2 = comb.mul %0, %1 : i9
    %3 = comb.concat %c0_i5, %c : i5, i4
    %4 = comb.add %2, %3 : i9
    hw.output %4 : i9
  }
}
```

::: {.fragment}
The operation mnemonic starts with its dialect: `hw.module`, `comb.mul`,
`comb.add`. Integer types such as `i4` and `i9` are built into MLIR.
:::

## Save the IR for the next tools {#tools-save-ir}

```bash
circt-verilog rtl/fma.sv -o rtl/fma.mlir
```

::: {.incremental}
- Without `-o`, use the terminal to inspect a transformation immediately.

- With `-o`, keep an intermediate representation for another pass or tool.

- The file is text: inspect it with `less`, `vim`, or `nano`.
:::

## Optimize with `circt-opt` {#tools-optimize}

```bash
circt-opt rtl/fma.mlir \
  --comb-int-range-narrowing \
  --canonicalize \
  -o rtl/fma_opt.mlir
```

| Pass | What it does here |
|---|---|
| `--comb-int-range-narrowing` | Proves that a 4-bit by 4-bit multiplication fits in 8 bits |
| `--canonicalize` | Removes redundant extensions, truncations, and other local structure |

::: {.fragment}
CIRCT is a compiler stack: flows are composed from **passes**.
:::

## The optimized FMA {#tools-optimized-ir}

```mlir
module {
  hw.module @fma(
      in %a : i4, in %b : i4, in %c : i4,
      out d : i9) {
    %false = hw.constant false
    %c0_i4 = hw.constant 0 : i4
    %0 = comb.concat %c0_i4, %a : i4, i4
    %1 = comb.concat %c0_i4, %b : i4, i4
    %2 = comb.mul %0, %1 : i8
    %3 = comb.concat %c0_i4, %c : i4, i4
    %4 = comb.add %2, %3 : i8
    %5 = comb.concat %false, %4 : i1, i8
    hw.output %5 : i9
  }
}
```

The arithmetic is now eight bits wide; only the module output is extended to
nine bits.

## Exercise 1 - pass order - 2 min {#tools-exercise-1}

Swap the two passes:

```bash
circt-opt rtl/fma.mlir \
  --canonicalize \
  --comb-int-range-narrowing \
  -o rtl/fma_swapped.mlir

diff -u rtl/fma_opt.mlir rtl/fma_swapped.mlir
```

**How does the output change? Why could the second pass order leave more IR?**

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.fragment}
**Answer:** narrowing first exposes redundant extensions to `canonicalize`.
When canonicalization runs first, narrowing later introduces `comb.extract`
operations and an extra output `comb.concat` that are not cleaned up again.
:::
:::

## Do you trust the transformation? {#tools-lec-intro}

> Of course, you do not trust research tools.

::: {.fragment}
And industrial tools are always exact, except when their documentation lists
[IEEE-754 partial compliance](https://docs.amd.com/r/en-US/ug1399-vitis-hls/Floats-and-Doubles)
and
[deviations](https://docs.amd.com/api/khub/documents/ym1A7qsltTGP_saZFTrikQ/content).
:::

::: {.fragment}
CIRCT lets us mark our own homework with a logical equivalence checker:
`circt-lec`.
:::

## Verify with `circt-lec` {#tools-lec}

General form:

```bash
circt-lec --c1 <module_1> <design_1.mlir> \
          --c2 <module_2> <design_2.mlir>
```

Our FMA:

```bash
circt-lec --c1 fma rtl/fma.mlir \
          --c2 fma rtl/fma_opt.mlir
```

```text
c1 == c2
```

## How does `circt-lec` work? {#tools-lec-how}

::: {.incremental}
1. Construct a **miter** that drives both circuits with the same inputs and
   compares their outputs.

2. Lower the miter and both modules to SMT.

3. Ask Z3 whether an input can make the outputs differ.

4. `unsat` means there is no counterexample: `c1 == c2`.
:::

::: {.fragment}
CIRCT also provides bounded model checking through `circt-bmc`; this tutorial
stays with combinational equivalence.
:::

## Exercise 2 - break the circuit - 5 min {#tools-exercise-2}

1. Copy `rtl/fma_opt.mlir` to a new file.
2. Break the copied IR with `vim` or `nano`.
3. Compare it with the original using `circt-lec`.
4. Check that the result is `c1 != c2`.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.fragment}
Change the multiply to an add, alter a constant, or disconnect an operand.
The current tool reports inequivalence but does not conveniently print the
counterexample.
:::
:::

## Generate Verilog with `firtool` {#tools-firtool}

A classic CIRCT flow is:

1. Parse a design into CIRCT IR.
2. Optimize the IR and verify the transformations.
3. Emit Verilog for downstream FPGA or ASIC tools.

```bash
firtool rtl/fma_opt.mlir
```

```systemverilog
module fma(
  input  [3:0] a, b, c,
  output [8:0] d
);
  assign d = {1'h0,
    {4'h0, a} * {4'h0, b} + {4'h0, c}};
endmodule
```

## Exercise 3 - round trip - 5 min {#tools-exercise-3}

1. Modify the `firtool` command to save the generated Verilog.
2. Compile that Verilog back to CIRCT IR with `circt-verilog`.
3. Use `circt-lec` to prove that the round trip preserved equivalence.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.fragment}
```bash
firtool rtl/fma_opt.mlir -o rtl/fma_roundtrip.sv
circt-verilog rtl/fma_roundtrip.sv -o rtl/fma_roundtrip.mlir
circt-lec --c1 fma rtl/fma_opt.mlir \
          --c2 fma rtl/fma_roundtrip.mlir
```
:::
:::

## Tutorial Part 2: datapath synthesis {#tools-datapath-part}

::: {.incremental}
1. Convert word-level arithmetic to the `datapath` dialect.

2. Expose partial products and compressor trees.

3. Synthesize the design to an And-Inverter Graph.

4. Export AIGER for downstream logic synthesis.
:::

## Why expose the datapath? {#tools-datapath-motivation}

For a dot product `(a * b) + (c * d)`:

| Direct structure | Fused datapath |
|---|---|
| Reduce each multiplication separately | Generate all partial products first |
| Two compressor trees | One shared compressor tree |
| Three carry-propagate additions | One final carry-propagate addition |

::: {.fragment}
For small widths the gain may be modest; at larger widths, the arithmetic
structure gives the optimizer more useful choices.
:::

## Compile the dot product {#tools-dot-product}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```systemverilog
// rtl/dot_product.sv
module dot_product (
  input wire [7:0] a, b, c, d,
  output wire [15:0] out
);
  assign out = (a * b) + (c * d);
endmodule
```
:::

::: {.column width="54%"}
```bash
circt-verilog rtl/dot_product.sv \
  -o rtl/dot_product.mlir
```

```mlir
%ab = comb.mul %a16, %b16 : i16
%cd = comb.mul %c16, %d16 : i16
%out = comb.add %ab, %cd : i16
```
:::
::::

## Dialect conversion is a transformation {#tools-dialect-conversion}

::: {.incremental}
- Some passes convert operations between dialects.

- This is often called **lowering**, because compilation usually moves toward
  lower-level representations.

- A dialect conversion can also promote information to a higher-level form.

- CIRCT pass names commonly follow `--convert-<source>-to-<target>`.
:::

```bash
circt-opt rtl/dot_product.mlir \
  --convert-comb-to-datapath
```

## Before canonicalization {#tools-convert-datapath}

```mlir
// a * b
%abParts:16 = datapath.partial_product %a16, %b16
  : (i16, i16) -> (i16, i16, i16, i16,
                    i16, i16, i16, i16,
                    i16, i16, i16, i16,
                    i16, i16, i16, i16)
%abRows:2 = datapath.compress %abParts#0, ...,
  %abParts#15 : i16 [16 -> 2]
%ab = comb.add bin %abRows#0, %abRows#1 : i16

// c * d gets another 16 rows and another compressor.
%out = comb.add %ab, %cd : i16
```

The conversion exposes the implementation, but it has not yet used the known
eight-bit operand ranges.

## Optimization opportunities {#tools-datapath-opportunities}

::: {.incremental}
1. Why did an eight-bit multiplication produce **16 partial products**?

2. Do the two products need separate `datapath.compress` operations?

3. Do we need a carry-propagate addition for each product before adding them?
:::

```bash
circt-opt rtl/dot_product.mlir \
  --convert-comb-to-datapath \
  --canonicalize
```

## After canonicalization {#tools-datapath-fused}

```mlir
%abParts:8 = datapath.partial_product %a16, %b16
  : (i16, i16) -> (i16, i16, i16, i16,
                    i16, i16, i16, i16)
%cdParts:8 = datapath.partial_product %c16, %d16
  : (i16, i16) -> (i16, i16, i16, i16,
                    i16, i16, i16, i16)

%rows:2 = datapath.compress
  %abParts#0, ...,
  %abParts#7, %cdParts#0, ...,
  %cdParts#7 : i16 [16 -> 2]
%out = comb.add bin %rows#0, %rows#1 : i16
```

Eight useful rows per multiplier, one compressor, one final addition.

## Exercise 4 - read the datapath - 15 min {#tools-exercise-4}

1. Determine what computation `rtl/ex4.mlir` implements.
2. Write `rtl/ex4_mine.sv` implementing that computation.
3. Import your SystemVerilog and prove equivalence with `circt-lec`.
4. Apply `--canonicalize --convert-datapath-to-comb`. What happened?

**Hint:** `extract`, `replicate`, and `concat` implement sign extension:

```systemverilog
wire [8:0] sext_a = {{5{a[3]}}, a};
```

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.fragment}
```systemverilog
assign d = $signed(a) * $signed(b) + $signed(c);
```

Converting back to `comb` expands the signed partial products and reduction
network into explicit bit-vector logic.
:::
:::

## Logic synthesis with `circt-synth` {#tools-synthesize}

`circt-synth` lowers the design toward gate-level `synth` operations. Its
default low-level representation is an And-Inverter Graph.

```bash
circt-synth rtl/dot_product.mlir \
  --analysis-output=analysis \
  --analysis-output-format=text \
  -o rtl/dot_product_aig.mlir
```

```text
Resource Usage Analysis for module: dot_product
  <unknown>:          33
  synth.aig.and_inv: 976

Longest Path Analysis result for "dot_product"
Maximum path level: 33
```

These are structural estimates, not technology-mapped area and timing.

## Export AIGER {#tools-aiger}

```bash
circt-translate rtl/dot_product_aig.mlir \
  --export-aiger \
  -o rtl/dot_product.aiger
```

AIGER can be consumed by tools such as
[ABC](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~alanmi/abc/) and
[Yosys](https://github.com/YosysHQ/yosys) for technology mapping toward FPGA
or ASIC libraries.

::: {.fragment}
Export from the **`circt-synth` result**, not directly from the word-level IR
generated by `circt-verilog`.
:::

## Exercise 5 - beat 54 AIG nodes - 15 min {#tools-exercise-5}

1. Parse `rtl/ex5.sv` and synthesize an AIG. How many And-Inverter nodes does
   it use?
2. Copy the SystemVerilog and optimize it **by hand**.
3. Can you beat Sam's result of **54 And-Inverter nodes**?
4. Prove your optimized design equivalent to the original with `circt-lec`.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.fragment}
The four branches are one conditional inversion followed by an increment:

```systemverilog
assign out = (x ^ {8{a}}) + b;
```

With the pinned image: **149 -> 54** AIG nodes and **13 -> 8** logic levels.
:::
:::

## CIRCT command glossary {#tools-glossary}

| Tool | Role in the tutorial |
|---|---|
| `circt-verilog` | Parse SystemVerilog and emit CIRCT IR |
| `circt-opt` | Run CIRCT and MLIR passes |
| `circt-lec` | Prove two CIRCT modules logically equivalent |
| `firtool` | Emit Verilog from CIRCT IR |
| `circt-synth` | Synthesize CIRCT IR to lower-level logic |
| `circt-translate` | Export formats such as AIGER |
| `z3` | Solve the equivalence query generated by `circt-lec` |

## Extension: from `arith` to hardware {#tools-arith-part}

The original five exercises began from SystemVerilog. We now add the course's
new arithmetic exercise.

::: {.incremental}
1. Express an E4M3 multiplication as one `arith.mulf`.

2. Match that operation in an out-of-tree CIRCT pass.

3. Build the corresponding `comb` datapath.

4. Specialize `%x * %x` into a squarer.
:::

## The complete RTL is the executable reference {#tools-complete-reference}

```bash
circt-verilog examples/e4m3fn-mul.sv \
  -o build/e4m3fn-mul-complete.mlir

./scripts/test-e4m3-all.py
```

```text
Testing all 65,536 input pairs
PASS: all 65536 E4M3 products match MLIR
```

The reference covers round-to-nearest-even, zeros, subnormals, overflow, and
signed NaNs. Students can inspect its generated `comb` network.

## Return to one `arith.mulf` {#tools-back-to-arith}

```mlir
hw.module @e4m3fn_mul(
    in %lhs : i8, in %rhs : i8,
    out result : i8) {
  %lhsf = arith.bitcast %lhs : i8 to f8E4M3FN
  %rhsf = arith.bitcast %rhs : i8 to f8E4M3FN
  %product = arith.mulf %lhsf, %rhsf : f8E4M3FN
  %result = arith.bitcast %product : f8E4M3FN to i8
  hw.output %result : i8
}
```

The pass must now choose the architecture that the RTL reference wrote by
hand.

## Match the complete floating-point island {#tools-pass-shape}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```cpp
class LowerE4M3FNMulPattern
    : public OpRewritePattern<arith::BitcastOp> {
  LogicalResult matchAndRewrite(
      arith::BitcastOp outputCast,
      PatternRewriter &rewriter) const override {
    auto mul = outputCast.getIn()
        .getDefiningOp<arith::MulFOp>();
    auto lhsCast = mul.getLhs()
        .getDefiningOp<arith::BitcastOp>();
    auto rhsCast = mul.getRhs()
        .getDefiningOp<arith::BitcastOp>();
    // Build an i8 comb network.
  }
};
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
The root is the output bitcast:

::: {.incremental}
- `arith.mulf` produces `f8E4M3FN`.

- The new `comb` network produces `i8`.

- At the outer bitcast, the replacement type already agrees.
:::
:::
::::

## Exercise 6 - lower E4M3 - 30 min {#tools-exercise-6}

Edit `lib/LowerE4M3FNToComb.cpp`:

1. Extract sign, exponent, and fraction from both operands.
2. Build hidden-bit significands and the four-by-four `comb.mul`.
3. Implement exponent adjustment and normal-path normalization.
4. Pack the result and test selected normal values.
5. Add rounding and exceptional values, then run the exhaustive checker.

```bash
./scripts/test-e4m3-all.py --pass
```

## Exercise 7 - specialize `x * x` - 15 min {#tools-square-exercise}

1. Match a multiply whose operands are the same SSA value.
2. Decode the operand only once.
3. Make finite and zero result signs constant zero.
4. Preserve the input sign when propagating NaN.
5. Emit a dedicated four-bit significand squarer.
6. Prove equivalence and compare AIG area and depth.
